passage: In the research institute's canteen, Tanuja finally said it to Dr Zeenat, her supervisor. "I think I'm a fraud. Everyone in the lab seems to understand the models instantly. Her tea had gone cold. She laughed anyway.

Dear Tanvir,
Thank you for last Tuesday. I nearly didn't tell you. I'd rehearsed saying "the new role is going fine" all morning. Then you asked how I was really doing, and it came out: that I feel like I'm acting, that one day the board will realise I only got this job because the other candidate withdrew. I expected you to reassure me politely. Instead you told me about your first year as a director, sitting in your car before meetings, sure you'd be found out. And that half the people on your leadership course had said the same. I can't describe the relief. The feeling didn't vanish. It just stopped being a shameful secret and became something ordinary, something people like you carry too. I slept properly on Tuesday for the first time in weeks.
Sudha

For a year at the architecture firm, I carried a secret. I was sure I'd been hired by mistake. Every compliment felt like a trap. I'm Ishita, and I didn't tell anyone, because saying it out loud felt like admitting it was true.
Then one evening, after a late review, my mentor Raghav asked how I was doing. I heard myself say, “I feel like a fraud. I think you're all going to find out.”
I expected him to look disappointed. Instead he laughed, kindly. “Welcome to the club. I felt that way until I was thirty-five. Half the partners feel it before every pitch.”
I was stunned. Raghav had designed buildings I'd studied in college.
Afterwards, the feeling didn't vanish. But it lost its power. It wasn't a secret sign of my failure anymore. It was just something a lot of good people carry.

qa.a: He felt that way until he was thirty-five.

qa.a: Ishita felt stunned and relieved, as the feeling stopped seeming like a secret sign of failure.

After the staff meeting on Tuesday, she stayed back with Karthik sir, the senior botany lecturer. She hadn't planned to say it. "Sir, I feel like I'm pretending. Like I got this job by mistake."
